title: Rework null bits
body:
**Changes**:
This PR reworks null bits in the storage and query processor: Null bits are organized as uint64_t entries both in the physical storage and `NullMask` (used by `ValueVector`), and each entry consists of 64 bits, one bit for each element.
In physical pages, null entries are placed directly after element values.

This change is to optimize the scan of null bits from pages to ValueVector's `NullMask`, instead of setting one element at a time, when the scan is sequential, we can align and set the whole null entry one at a time.

title: orderBy string optimization
body:
This PR does the following optimizations for orderBy string column:
1.  OrderByScan: 
- Instead of encoding 6 bytes for tupleIdx and 2 bytes for factorizedTableIdx. We do: 4 bytes encoding for factorizedTableBlockIdx, 3 bytes encoding for factorizedTableBlockOffset, 1 byte for factorizedTableIdx. This can accelerate the fetching the string from the factorizedTable because we no longer need to do a division and mod operation to calculate the tuplePtr in factorizedTable. The drawBack is that the 1 byte encoding limits our maximum number of threads to 256.
- We encode one more byte for strings to indicate whether this string is a long or a short string. The new encoding length for string will be 14 bytes (1byte null + 12 bytes prefix  + 1byte long/short flag)
- EncodeTuples() for loop optimization

2. Radix sort:
- Instead of fetching the actual string from factorizedTable for each string comparison in quickSort, we can utilize the encoded long/short string flag to minimize the number of string fetch from factorizedTable.
- FindTies() for loop change to minimize the number of multiplications.

3. KeyBlockMerger:
- Minimizes the number of times of fetching strings from factorizedTable by utilizing the long/short string flag in compareTuplePtr().

4. FactorizedTable:
- Table schema now stores the numBytesPerTuple. We don't need to calculate the numBytesPerTuple dynamically during getNumBytesPerTuple().
- Change the getCell() interface. Instead of dynamically getting the colOffset, getCell() now takes in a colOffset parameter.

The main logic of Column::updateFixedLenPartAndReturnUpdatedPageInfoAndWALPageFrame is in StorageStructure::getUpdatePageInfoForElementAndCreateWALVersionOfPageIfNecessary. 

- OverflowPages::writeStringOverflowAndUpdateOverflowPtr: This handles writing a new string to the overflow file. Currently the logic is very simple and leaves holes in the pages of OverflowPages. We keep a single pointer called nextBytePosToWriteTo. This keeps track of the last available position in the pages where an overflow string can be written (can be used for lists too). Then we simply write to this space and increment nextBytePosToWriteTo. So this pointer monotonically increases and when previous overflows become "dangling" we don't have a mechanism to reuse them.

- WALReplayer: This change is minor. The only additional change is that modifications to string can create new page insertions. We need to treat page insertions differently than updates because if an insertion rolls back, we want to "undo" the insertion by truncating the fileHandle back to its previous size. Note that this truncation logic is currently very simple: Since we assume there is only a single write transaction in the system at any point in time, if we are undoing the insertion of page 5, we can truncate the file directly to 5 pages. That is suppose page 5 and page 6 were added during a transaction but then the transaction rolls back. In the WAL, when we replay, we will first see page 5 insertion. When we see page 5 insertion, we can directly remove both page 5 and page 6 from the fileHandle. This is because we assume that any further new page additions, i.e. those with higher page indices, must also be part of the rolling back transaction, so we can simply remove those pages from the MultiVersionFileHandle for the StorageStructure too. This is also explained inside a comment in WALReplayer.

Main Abstraction Changes:
MultiVersionFileHandle: This takes the logic of keeping pageLocks and pageVersion info data from Column to a new class MultiVersionFileHandle. This allows us to also keep one lock per page, instead of two locks. Previously we had a class called PageVersionInfo, which kept a second lock for each page P in a page group PG that had at least one update. This second lock was stored in the pageLocksAndVersionsPerPageGroup field of PageVersionInfo and was not necessary. MultiVersionFileHandle is meant to be used for any storage structure whose pages might be backed up by WAL pages. Although Lists don't yet need MultiVersionFileHandle, to simplify the class hierarchy, by default any storage structure, so Column, List, or OverflowPages (see the note below that OverflowPages also now extend StorageStructure), have a MultiVersionFileHandle instead of a FileHandle. 

Related to the changes in the FileHandle: FileHandle also now contains new functions to decrease the numPages (and resize the managed data structures). These were not needed before. They are now needed in case a transaction makes updates, which may increase the number of pages in the overflows but then rolls back, so we need to take the filehandle back to its previous state.

BaseColumnOrList: Previous StorageStructure is now called BaseColumnOrList. This class further extends another class called StorageStructure. This class holds some common fields between Column, Lists, and OverflowPages, such as bufferManager, wal, fileHandle, isInMemory. This was initially needed to share some update logic between Column and OverflowPages but once we needed yet even a more basic class, I used it to store common fields as well.

OverflowBufferUtils: Moved the utility functions in TypeUtils that handled overflow-related operations from TypeUtils to a new class OverflowBufferUtils. This was needed because OvrerflowBuffer depends on BufferManager which depends on something etc. and was causing a circular dependency when OverflowPages included type_utils.h

Also removes AdjColumnFileID related log structs from wal_record.h. These were not used and slows us down as many abstractions change as we figure out the right classes to abstract the general logic of transactions.

title: checkpointing logic
body:
Adds checkpointing logic for a committed transactions. The logic is currently implemented in database.h temporarily. That is because in absence of the frontend, the current tests do not use the connection class to interact with the db using transactions. Instead, we manually create transactions by calling transactionManager::beginWriteTransaction etc. Ideally this logic should go to connection.cpp. The logic is this:

For a write transaction that is committing:
1. write ahead the wal to disk
2. wait until all other running (read-only) transactions leave the system
3. commit (but keep the active transaction alive because currently each commit is immediately followed by a checkpoint)
4. storageManager::checkpoint()
5. truncate the wal to empty (by calling wal::clearWAL.
6. clear active transaction
7. allow new transactions to come in the system

For a write transaction that is rolling back:
only steps 6 and 7 run.

We currently have the logic to error and rollback if waiting for existing transactions to leave the system. This will be better tested when we start testing transactions through connection. For example we don't currently test that after this error the transaction is rolled back and wal is cleared etc, which will automatically happen through the connection. 
 
Checkpointing Algorithm:
This is implemented in a new WALReplayer (wal_replayer.h/cpp) class and is straightforward: We loop over each log and redo during checkpointing.  WALReplayer is also used for rolling back to undo some operations and these two algorithms share code. Although database files are guaranteed to not be updated during WAL, other structures, such as PageVersionInfo, can be updated and need to be undone. WALReplayer can be constructed either in checkpoint or rollback mode and in both modes call the same replay() function which for checkpointing does the extra work of copying over updates from WAL pages to the original db files and in both modes replay() also undoes the changes to the PageVersionInfo (and later possibly other structures).

title: Hash index concurrent insertions
body:
This PR adds support for concurrent insertion after `bulkReserve` in HashIndex.
Also, cached blocks are changed to be managed through BufferManager. During flushing, cached blocks are marked as dirty, and will be flushed to disk by BufferManager.

The insertion locking scheme is that:
for each primary and ovf slot, there is a mutex, i.e., `primarySlotMutexes`, and `ovfSlotMutexes`. Access to a slot during insertion requires a lock first.
When a key is to be inserted, we first calculate its primary slot id, based on which, we will require its lock and read its header. Remind that the way we organize our slots is each primary slot is chained with a list of ovf slots. So during insertion, to find the correct slot for insertion, we follow the chain by acquiring the nextOvfSlot's lock, and releasing the previous one. In this way, we can minimize the impact of locking.

Ovf page allocation:
During insertion, when a primary/ovf slot is full, we need to allocate a new ovf slot to address the hash confliction. The allocation happens in two cases: 1) there are empty ovf slots available in a ovf page, we require a global lock, and increment the current soltId to the empty one; 2) there are no empty ovf slots available, we need to allocate a new ovf page. We first require a global lock, then acquire a lock on `ovfSharedMutex`, which coordinates accesses to ovf pages, i.e., `ovfCachedBlocks`. The double locking design is to minimize the conflict between reading a slot from `ovfCachedBlocks`, and allocating a new ovf page.

title: fix deadlock in LIST overflow
body:
This is a fix to the deadlock bug when we load LIST values. Thanks to @acquamarin for reporting this bug.

The bug is due to incorrect locking inside `InMemOverflowPages`.  Previously, `InMemOverflowPages::addList` acquires a shared lock first before copying list elements, suppose each LIST element is a string, `InMemOverflowPages::copyVarSizedValuesToPages` will call `addString`, which will call `InMemOverflowPages::copyStringOverflow`, and acquire an exclusive lock when it needs a new page. The deadlock happens here, the thread is holding a shared lock already, thus, it will block trying to acquire the exclusive lock.

title: Add abstract table scan and physical set.
body:
This PR contains multiple changes related to physical set operator.

# Phyiscal Operators
## Set
The physical set operator itself is a pipelined operator which updates a property column to an expression evaluation result for each input nodeID. This initial implementation only supports node structured property. To avoid undefined behavior as stated in the design doc. We append a ResultCollector and a FactorizedTableScan before each sink.

## ResultCollector
Add getMorsel() interface to allow multi-thread scanning from factorized table

## BaseTableScan, FactorizedTableScan and UnionAll
Abstract common table scan interface in to BaseTableScan operator. FactorizedTableScan scans from 1 factorized table while UnionAll scans from multiple factorized table.

# Logical Operators
## Remove logical result collector
In our design pattern, sink and scan operators are generated together. The only exception is a result collector will also be appended at the very end of a physical plan. Therefore, we should not define a logical result collector.
## LogicalSinkScan
This operator represents the ResultCollector and FactorizedTableScan we append before Set operator. Its name is subject to change.


# For Reviewers
- See if removing logical result collector decision is justified.
- Review all changes under physical_plan/operator
- Review if it makes sense to have ResultCollector and FTableScan as its own operator instead of making Set being able to sink/scan.

title: Update of structured properties and basic WAL functionality
body:
Implements the backend for updating structured node properties. Gets in some infrastructure code to ensure updates are logged to a WAL and writer transactions see what they wrote without affecting read transactions.

Main New/Modified Classes:
WAL, WALIterator and WALRecord: Implement log record structures needed for updating columns and a library to write log records and iterate over log records.
Column: is modified to take as an argument during construction a WAL. Column also now has a function that can update the column, which leads to possibly writing a page to WAL and logging a record to WAL. Columns read functions also take in a transaction now, which is used to know which version of a page a transaction should read: readOnly transactions read the default page in the db file, while the writing transaction reads possibly from the WAL. 
PageVersionInfo: Is used to keep track of whether a particular page in a Column has multiple version or a single version. Implements the existing design.
There are several tests for these classes.

Medium Level Change:
Catalog: Catalog's way of holding information for Properties used to be in a class called PropertyDefinition that stored its string name, id, data type, and whether the property is the primary key or not. This is also used by the loader and several fields would be empty or not used previously. We needed to pass more information to Columns to log the ID of the file that Column uses to store data. We could use the string name but it would mean that we log the string in the wal logs. This could be fine but does not look right. To pass the necessary information to Column we need to pass the label of the nodes and when the column stores single multiplicity edges, i.e., the column is an adj column or holds properties of such single multiplicity edges, then also the rel label. This PR implements a new struct Property that stores more information about a property and passes it down to the coluimn.

The PR also solves a separate bug that I ran into, in which we were not reading the NULL bits for node offsets > 8 in the columns and directly setting their values to null. This bug is fixed and the PR modifies some input datasets we use to contain nulls in their structured properties to test this case now.

title: Making the scheduling thread wait for all threads to finish during errors.
body:
We used to remove a task in which at least one worker thread errored from the task queue. This means that by the time the application is notified that there is an exception in the query another worker thread could still be working on a pipeline of this query. This can be a problem when we implement transactions. For example, when we implement transactions, the connection could rollback a transaction but the "continuing worker thread" can still have a handle to this transaction and use it to scan data etc. 
This PR does the safer thing and ensures that no worker thread is working no any task related to the query before the application is notified.

title: Transactions Warm Up
body:
This PR adds basic support for beginning, committing, and rolling back transactions. Major classes that are added or modified are:

- Connection

The general behavior is explained in the comment above TransactionMode inside connection (copy pasted as it is in the current version of the PR):

    /**
     * If the connection is in AUTO_COMMIT mode any query over the connection will be wrapped around
     * a transaction and committed (even if the query is READ_ONLY).
     * If the connection is in MANUAL transaction mode, which happens only if an application
     * manually begins a transaction (see below), then an application has to manually commit or
     * rollback the transaction by calling commit() or rollback().
     *
     * AUTO_COMMIT is the default mode when a Connection is created. If an application calls
     * begin[ReadOnly/Write]Transaction at any point, the mode switches to MANUAL. This creates
     * an "active transaction" in the connection. When a connection is in MANUAL mode and the
     * active transaction is rolled back or committed, then the active transaction is removed (so
     * the connection no longer has an active transaction) and the mode automatically switches
     * back to AUTO_COMMIT.
     * Note: If connection is closed() and the connection has an active (manual) transaction, then
     * the active transaction is rolled back.
     */

## Change function overloading signatures
For overloaded functions with known output type (e.g. `sin(INT) -> DOUBLE`  & `sin(DOUBLE) -> DOUBLE`), we use to have unstructured overloding signature as `sin(VALUE) -> VALUE`. This PR changes the signature to `sin(VALUE) -> DOUBLE`

## Change Cypher grammar-defined arithmetic and string functions to use function framework.
Previously we bind Cypher grammar-defined arithmetic and string functions (i.e. `+, -, *, /, %, ^, CONTAINS, STARTS_WITH`) with its own logic. This PR generates signatures for these functions and bind them through our new framework. As a consequence, we remove their expression type and treat them as regular functions. 

We did a similar change to Cypher grammar-defined  comparison functions (i.e. `=, <>, > , >=, <, <=`). But we keep their expression type.

title: Non-nested LIST loading
body:
This PR adds support for loading non-nested LIST into our system.
The scan/read of LIST in the query processor is not yet added, so the test is directly on the storage side for now.
The supported data types inside a LIST (i.e., its child data type) are BOOL, INT64, DOUBLE, STRING, TIMESTAMP, DATE, and INTERVAL. Currently, we don't support LIST of LIST or UNSTRUCTURED values.

1. The CSVReader is changed to parse list in CSV files by reusing existing CSVReader for each list substring in a single line, after parsing, the list is temporarily stored as a `Literal` (see `getList` function) and later be passed to be loaded.
2. The PropertyDefinition adds one more field: childDataType to indicate the LIST's child data type.
3. The NodesLoader and RelsLoader add changes to copy LISTs into mem pages. The layout of a LIST of STRING in the overflow page is [gf_string_t,...,gf_string_t,overflow_origianl_string,...,overflow_original_string]. Inside the overflow page, we always store the gf_string_t before the original overflow string.

This PR also introduces some minor renamings and refactorings as I go along my changes:
- Move CSV related special chars or configuration to `CSVReaderConfig`.


Cases not handled yet:
- Nulls in the LIST.
- Sort LIST overflows in rel columns/lists.

title: Changing in memory db mode to not use BM instead of OS memory
body:
Fixes the first item in https://github.com/graphflowdb/graphflowdb/issues/494. 

When we run the system in memory mode, the FileHandles to the database files used to use a unique_ptr<uint8_t[]> buffer; and read a file directly into this buffer. For example, if a column takes 1G, we'd acquire a 1G array through the OS. Instead we now pin the pages of this file in the BM when constructing Column and Lists. Then the rest of the access to these pages go through the BM as before. 

Note that we are losing some performance here because we still acquire locks when accessing the page but we do not do any I/O, so a cache hit is guaranteed. So the performance is similar to when we have a large BM. 

For now, I made this decision to go for simplicity. If later we decide to be very careful about the performance of the in-memory db mode, there is an easy buffer manager interface extension that can avoid any locks. We would have a separate pinInMemoryPage function, which would pin the page once and be called (as in this PR) from DataStructure's base constructor. Then we would have special case if (isInMemory) branches into the original pin and unpin function in BufferPool. For example, for unpin, as was done previously, if the file isInMemory, we'd just return. pin would require a bit more work. Probably we'd skip over the part of pin that acquires the page lock and the rest would be the same.

As an independent change 1: I had to test the BM's behavior through the embedded shell, so added a few new commands to the shell to see debug information about the bm and the system overall. I also changed how command line arguments are parsed in the shell_runner to make it more robust to order of arguments. I used the command line argument parser library that was done in the loader (@Taywee_args).

As an independent change 2: Renames data_structure folder and build package to storage_structure.

title: Multi page size bm
body:
This PR changes several things about the BufferManager's (BM) internals and how it can be used: 

- BM now supports 2 different page sizes: DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE and LARGE_PAGE_SIZE, both defined in configs.h. Currently these values are 4K and 256K but can be configured. This is done by extracting the main functionalities of the BM to a BufferPool class, and having the BufferManager class wrap 2 BufferPools. 
- Extends Frames with isDirty flag, which needs to be set explicitly through the BM. This leads to the BM writing these pages to disk when evicting.
- FileHandle has two new fields: 1) whether the pages of the file are largePaged or not; 2) whether the file is a new temporary file. These are done through a flag implementation, where several common flag configurations are added as constant in FileHandle.
- MemoryManager (MM) remains but for now has a new functionality to acquire its memory blocks through the BM.  This is only supported for fixed LARGE_PAGE_SIZE memory blocks. The previous functionality of acquiring memory through the OS still remains for now and should eventually be deprecated (adde these TODOs). So users can call MM::allocateBMBackedBlock, which will give to the user a page of size LARGE_PAGE_SIZE. These memories are never spilled to disk and the MM keeps them pinned. So the callers are guaranteed that these memory blocks will remain in memory. The implication of this is that MM has an internal FileHandle (that is configured to be isNewTmp and isLargePaged). When allocateBMBackedBlock is called, it sees if there is a free page in the file, and if so, just pins the page. Then a separate MM::freeBMBackedBlock function needs to be called to give these memories back to the system. MM will then unpin these pages.
- As an example of how to use BM-backed memory during query processing, StringBuffer is reimplemented to now use MM's allocateBMBackedBlock functions instead of allocateOSBackedBlock (which is a rename of the previous allocateBlock function).
- As part of these changes, makes BM and MM usage through shared_ptr's. This was needed primarily because some tests, that were constructing their own BufferManager and MemoryManagers were failing, because it is not easy to understand/control which sequence of destructors are called across FileHandle, StringBuffer, MM, and BM, when these are raw pointers. The problem was that the BM or MM would be deconstructed before StringBuffer, which would then try to free pages, which would cause seg faults. Keeping shared pointers guarantees that BufferManager and/or MemoryManager cannot be deconstructed before StringBuffer.
- As an independent change, makes BufferManagerMetrics local to BufferManager instead of a query-specific metric. This has not been useful so far and I don't expect it to be very useful for a while. We were passing all around just so that a few operators would need to call pin/unpin through Column/List, and it has been slowing down our implementation speed.

More work needs to be done in the system to move large all OS-backed memory allocations (excluding small a few KB allocations, e.g., those done in ValueVector) to BM-backed ones again using MemoryManager. These are listed here: https://github.com/graphflowdb/graphflowdb/issues/494.

  -  execute(): collect tuples and update agg states. Once all tuples are collected, combine local state to global state.
  -  finalize(): finalize global state.

  -  execute(): collect tuples, hash group values and update states in dynamic agg hash table. Once all tuples are collected, move  local hash table to global.
  -  finalize(): create static agg hash table and combine state from local agg hash table. Finalize global hash table

Add aggregate hash table using linear probing for collision.

title: Projection map fix
body:
This PR resolves issue #376 and the second failed query in issue #430 

## Bug Description
In the previous design, we have a `dataChunkMask` in `ResultSet` which indicates which dataChunk is projected away. However, since our resultSet is shared, `dataChunkMask` can only reflect the final state instead of the intermediate state. This creates trouble when we have multiple projects.

## Changes
### ResultSet
- Remove `dataChunkMask`
- Change `getNumTuple()` to `getNumTuple(unorder_set<uint> dataChunksPosInScope)`
  -  The rationale is our project does not explicitly remove dataChunk. Therefore, whoever tries to read from multiple dataChunks needs to specify the positions. Blindly reading from all dataChunks is prohibited. 
- Add dataChunksPosInScope to operators  (both logical and physical) that might read from multiple dataChunks.
  -  Includes, SKIP, LIMIT, SIMPLE_AGGREGATE

title: New task scheduler that merges loader and processor thread pools.
body:
This PR does two things (the main contribution is 1) but 2) was a bug observed when testing 1), and I'm putting it in the same PR for now):

1) Addresses Issue #304. It merges the two thread pool components of loader and processor into a TaskScheduler that is under src/common. The TaskScheduler.h provides a detailed description of how different components (possibly other than loader and processor) can use the TaskScheduler to schedule a set of tasks that worker threads can execute in parallel. I am copy pasting it here:  


/**
* TaskScheduler is a library that manages a set of worker threads that can execute tasks that are
 * put into a task queue. Each task accepts a maximum number of threads. Users of TaskScheduler
 * schedule tasks to be executed by calling schedule functions, e.g., scheduleTask or
 * scheduleTaskAndWaitOrError. New tasks are put at the end of the queue. Workers grab the first
 * task from the beginning of the queue that they can register themselves to work on. Any task that
 * is completed is removed automatically from the queue. If there is a task that raises an
 * exception, the worker threads catch it and store it with the tasks. The user thread that is
 * waiting on the completion of the task (or tasks) will throw the exception (the user thread could
 * be waiting on a tasks through a function that waits, e.g., scheduleTaskAndWaitOrError or
 * waitAllTasksToCompleteOrError.
 *
 * Currently there are two ways the TaskScheduler can be used:
 * (1) Schedule a set of tasks T1, ..., Tk, and wait for all of them to be completed or error
 * if any one them has raised an exception (but only the exception of one (the earliest scheduled)
 * task will be raised. We do not currently re-throw multiple exceptions from multiple tasks. Ex:
 *      schedule(T1);
 *      ...;
 *      schedule(Tk);
 *      waitAllTasksToCompleteOrError();
 * (2) Schedule one task T and wait for T to finish or error if there was an exception raised by
 * one of the threads working on T that errored. This is simply done by the call:
 *      scheduleTaskAndWaitOrError(T);
 *
 * TaskScheduler guarantees that workers will register themselves to tasks in FIFO order. However
 * this does not guarantee that the tasks will be completed in FIFO order: a long running task
 * that is not accepting more registration can stay in the queue for an unlimited time until
 * completion.
 */

2) A minor-looking but important change to SimpleAggregate and SimpleAggregationScan, which were moving a shared pointer of their SharedState objects when cloning themselves. This meant that the reference physical plan P from which worker threads in the previous thread pool and current task_scheduler would clone, when cloning twice would run into segmentation or other errors. This is because after the first clone is called on the reference SimpleAggregate/SimpleAggregationScan, the move of the shared pointer removes the reference's co-ownership of SimpleAggregate/SimpleAggregationScan from the SharedState, so e.g., shared_ptr<AggregationSharedState> could be nullified. Therefore the second time clone is called, which happens when number of worker threads that can work on P is > 1, we would error. This bug existed in the previous thread pool, so is not related to the main change in this PR.

title: ID constraints and errors in loader.
body:
changes layout of file headers to follow neo4j's design. 

Earlier, header of a file used to be like `a:A,b:B,c:C` for both the node and rel files, where property a has dataType A and b has dataType B. Also for node files, we used to specify the primary key in the metadata file. however, contrary to node files, in rel files, from and to nodes (foreign keys) were still positional, that is, first and second column of the file.

Neo4j's design enforces node file to have header like `:ID,a:A,b:B` where `:ID` column specifies the unique identifier (primary key). And rel file header to be like `:START_ID,:END_ID,a:A,b:B`. the advantage of having special tags like :ID, :START_ID etc is that the primary (in node file) and foreign keys (in rel files) are not positional and neither needs to be defined in the metadata file for each label. 

This PR hence forms the basis for the next which will add the check to skip relationships which has invalid src or dst node ids.
Skipping nodes with duplicate node ids is not intuitive since technically we create the nodeIDMaps after inserting the properties of nodes. (while inserting properties, we parallelly create the reverse nodeIDMaps ) 

Also adds checks to verify if the csv header is correct and subsequently add tests for each case.

title: add null support for rowCollection
body:
To represent the null values in RowCollection, we use a bitmap to represent the null fields in each row
1. For overflow columns, we use a large bitmap to represent the nulls in the whole overflow columns and stores it at the end of the overflow memory.
2. For all other columns, we just store a bitmap at the end of each row.

For example:
we have 3 columns: a1   a2(overflow)   a3 = (1   [null,4,6,7]  null)     

                       
Since the 3rd column is a null value, we set the 3rd bit(from right to left) of the first byte to 1.
The memory of the row Collection looks like: 
1  overflowPtrToA2  0 nullMap:4(00000100).

Since the 1st element in the overflow column is a null value, we set the 1st bit(from right to left) of the first byte to 1.
The overflow column memory looks like: 
3 4 6 0 nullMap:1(00000001).

title: Issue 397
body:
This PR solves issue #397 

This PR introduces a design pattern for merging result sets from different branches (pipelines). For example, hash join probe result set need to merge hash join build result set. We might follow a similar pattern when merging subquery or scanning aggregation/order by tables. The pattern is described as following.

Build side takes a schema (BuildDataInfo) describing what vectors should be materialized. It contains
-  DataPos keyIDDataPos: describes the position of hash key.
-  vector<DataPos> nonKeyDataPoses: describes the positions of all payload vectors.

Probe side takes a schema (ProbeDataInfo) describing how to append build side payload to probe side. It contains
- DataPos keyIDDataPos: describe the position of hash key. On probe side, this hash key is only used for probing.
- vector<DataPos> nonKeyDataPoses: describes the appending positions of payload vectors.
  -  Note that build and probe side nonKeyDataPoses have one-to-one mapping which means we should scan all columns that are materialized. Otherwise those columns should not be part of the payload.

title: Refactor Exists Subquery
body:
This PR refactor the logic of exists subquery evaluation.

Previously, we had ExistsSubqueryExpressionEvaluator which could be part of the expression evaluator tree. The new design introduces Exists operator which evaluates a subquery plan for each input tuple. The evaluation result is written as a new value vector with true/false values depending on whether the subquery plan has at least one result or not. Similar to aggregation, exists subquery expression is evaluated by Exists operator and later on treated as a leaf expression in the expression evaluator tree.

This new design has the following advantage.

- Decoupling expression and logical plan/operator.
- Decoupling expression evaluator and physical plan/operator.
- Decoupling expression mapper and plan mapper
- Leave the potential to optimize the subquery plan together with the outer query plan. (If we keep subquery plan in ExistsSubqueryExpressionEvaluator, then we can only optimize plan layer by layer )

title: Add RowCollection and refactor hash join to use it
body:
This PR introduces `RowCollection`, an intermediate row-based data structure for the query result. It stores data in a row-fashion, which is mostly used by hash tables, and sink operators such as OrderBy to materialize intermediate results. 

HashJoin has been refactored to use RowCollection in this PR.

Each `RowCollection` requires a `RowLayout`, which is a "schema" describing, for each field, the size and if the vector should be stored as an overflow (e.g., unFlat vectors in non-key data chunks should be stored as overflow during the hash join building phase).

The `RowCollection` provides three interfaces to handle the transformation between vector-based ResultSet and row-based data blocks.
```
void append(const vector<shared_ptr<ValueVector>>& vectors, uint64_t numRowsToAppend);
uint64_t scan(const vector<uint64_t>& fieldsToScan, const vector<DataPos>& resultDataPos, ResultSet& resultSet, uint64_t startRowId, uint64_t numRowsToScan) const;
uint64_t lookup(const vector<uint64_t>& fieldsToRead, const vector<DataPos>& resultDataPos, ResultSet& resultSet, uint8_t** rowsToRead, uint64_t startPos, uint64_t numRowsToRead) const;
```

`scan` and `lookup` will return actual number of rows that is scanned from the row collection.

`scan` is responsible for scanning from the given logical `startRowId` to at most `startRowId + numRowsToScan`.
`lookup` takes in an array of pointers to physical rows, it will be responsible to read rows from `rowsToRead[startPos]` to at most `rowsToRead[startPos + numRowsToRead]`.

Given a startRowId, the actual number of rows to read are computed as follows:
```
numRowsToRead = min(numRowsToRead, numRows - startRowId); // bounded by remaining rows after the startRowId
numRowsToRead = min(hasVectorOverflow ? 1 : DEFAULT_VECTOR_CAPACITY, numRowsToRead); // bounded by if fields has vector overflow
```


This PR also generalizes `MorselDesc` to prepare it to be used for scans other than ScanNodeID.

Previously, leaf expression was defined as a set of expression types (PROPERTY, CSV_LINE_VARIABLE, ...) whose value is written to value vector before expression evaluation starts. This method is not correct since we could have an expression being aliased and become a leaf. For example, MATCH (a) WITH a.age + 2 AS newAge MATCH (b) RETURN b.age > newAge. In this case, newAge is a leaf expression when evaluating b.age > newAge.

This PR changes leaf expression to be an expression whose value exists in the schema, i.e., has been previously evaluated.  This is done through recursively check is a sub-expression exists in the schema or not

title: add encoder for order by
body:
Add encoder for order by operator.

The OrderByKeyEncoder encodes all columns in the ORDER BY clause into a single binary sequence that, when compared using memcmp will yield the correct overall sorting order.
On little-endian hardware, the least-significant byte is stored at the smallest address. To encode the sorting order, we need the big-endian representation for values.
For example: we want to encode 73(INT64) and 38(INT64) as an 8-byte binary string 
The encoding in little-endian hardware is:
73=0x4900000000000000 38=0x2600000000000000, which doesn't preserver the order. 
The encoding in big-endian hardware is: 
73=0x0000000000000049 38=0x0000000000000026, which can easily be compared using memcmp. 

In addition, The first bit is also flipped to preserve ordering between positive and negative numbers. 
So the final encoding for 73(INT64) and 38(INT64) as an 8-byte binary string: 
73=0x8000000000000049 38=0x8000000000000026 

If a string is too long, we only encode its prefix(12 bytes) and only look at the whole string if the prefixes are equal. 
With this binary string, we can now compare both columns at the same time by comparing only the binary string
representation.

To handle the null in comparison, we add an extra byte(called the NULL flag) to represent whether this value is null or not.
We currently add a null flag to all values, which affects the radix sort performance. We need to record whether or not a column has any nulls in catalog, so that we don't need add null flags to all values. Opened an issue about this #384.

title: fix over-large writes in writeToFile()
body:
Over-large writes will cause error when writing the file due to overflow (pwrite's `count` should be no greater than `SSIZE_MAX`, which is 32 bits) or partially write (On Linux, `write()` will transfer at most `0x7ffff000` (`2,147,479,552`) bytes).
In this PR, we split the write in `writeToFile()` to at most 1GB at a time, which is the same as our readFile, and large enough to get good io performance.

title: Refactor build files to avoid circular dependency of subquery expression.
body:
This PR refactor bazel build files to solve circular dependency introduced by subquery expression/evaluator.

### Circular dependency
Consider the case for expression_evaluator lib and physical_operator lib. 
- Expression_evaluator depends on physical_operator because subquery_evaluator requires the last operator of its subplan
- Physical_operator depends on expression_evaluator because filter/projection requires expression_evaluator
- In such case, bazel does know which lib to compile first.

### Solution
We create subquery_evaluator as its own lib. The updated dependency becomes
-  Physical_operator depends on expression_evaluator because filter/projection requires expression_evaluator
-  Subquery_evaluator depends on expression_evaluator
-  Subquery_evaluator depends on physical_operator
-  Compiling order becomes 
   -  expression_evaluator
   -  physical_operator
   -  subquery_evaluator
 
Same solution is applied to subquery_expression and logical_plan

### Additional change
Move clone() method from expression_mapper to expression_evaluator to decouple physical_operator and expression_mapper.
We used to compile physical_operator and expression_mapper together due to the clone() function. However, expression_mapper has to depend on subquery_evaluator while physical_operator can NOT depen on subquery_evaluator. So this decouple is needed.

title: grammar&binder support for subquery

## Binder Change

title: Subquery evaluator
body:
This PR adds ExistSubqueryEvaluator and SelectScan operator

## General Subquery Design
Inner subquery takes n value vectors as input from outer query. These inputs must be flat. So we run the subquery once for each input tuple.

### ExistSubqueryEvaluator
Holds the last operator of a subplan. Each call of evaluate() return true if subplan has at least one tuple.  This evaluator does NOT evaluate unflat input.

### SelectScan
Takes a vector of flat value vector as input and put them in a single flat dataChunk which becomes the input of subquery. Because SelectScan assumes single tuple input, on the second call of getNextTuple(), it terminates the execution of subplan.

title: Removes readBySettingFrame and simplifications to DataStructure, Lists, and Columns
body:
This PR does several refactoring and simplification at the interface of operators and storage, which is implemented in data_structure.h/cpp, lists.h/cpp, and column.h/cpp.

- Remove reading by settingFrame: All reads happen through copying. As a result we no longer need pageHandle.
- Fixes several hidden bugs in reading large lists due to how we were computing the sizeLeftToCopy for large lists. These fixes required introducing back the "originalSize" of data chunks before any filter for scans to use. If we push scans down this field may again become unnecessary. The core problem is that the we need to keep the vector sizes in data chunks the same length (which is the length of the original nodeIDSequence scan or the original 1-to-many extension). But if the scan happens after a filter, vectors become unaligned causing bugs. Adds some test data and tests for reading large property and adjacency lists. These bugs also highlighted a major performance bottleneck, for which I opened an issue #302, which should be fixed by pushing scans. See the issue for details.
- Removes templating from Lists and Columns: As part of this moves one common functions for columns, that was used by NodesStore and RelStore, into a ColumnFactory class.
- We still maintain what was called ListsPageHandle. This is now a wrapper around ListSyncState to support the "hasMoreRead" function which behaves differently if the ListSyncState is the state of an adj list or property list. This is now called LargeListHandle.
- Removes MAX_TO_READ. We always read as much as we can from a single page.


This PR also (and indepedently) fixes bugs in the threadpool that is used by the loader and the multi-threading code that is in the QueryProcessor. These classes do not use atomics any more and acquire locks before doing any operation and are written as libraries, so their fields are not exposed. In addition it fixes a minor bug in expression evaluator for unstructured properties (an rpos field should be lpos).

title: Re-implements nullmask, allowing for fast path execution for no-null cases

This PR extracts nullMasks in ValueVector to a new class that stores nullMask bool array as well as an additional bool mayContainNulls, that is false if the vector is guaranteed to not have nulls. This allows us to special case fast path executions that avoid null-related computation in executors. 
Other changes:
- NullMask bool array is no longer accessed directly but access through inline function calls to read and set nulls. These functions are in ValueVector instead of the NullMask class because some of these functions, e.g., `setAllNull`, require access to DataChunkState.
- Writes several tests to vector_comparison_operations and vector_arithmetic_operations to test the slow and fast paths, i.e., when the operands contain nulls and no nulls. Also extends some existing tests to verify that not only the result values are correct  but also their nullMasks are correct. 
- Refactors some common test code to construct DataChunk and ValueVectors in tests.
- An unrelated change that came up in this PR: Removed listLen from Lists::readValues and some other functions that readValues calls. This was a reference to DataChunkState->size, and was being set here (another reason we should have setters and getters instead of passing references), and was very difficult to track. We also realized this was not necessary since the ValueVector into which data will be read was being read was already passed to these functions as `const shared_ptr<ValueVector>& valueVector` argument, so we could set the size through this argument. So this argument was redundant.

title: Cyclic query support
body:
This PR add supports to cyclic queries and closes issue #140 

Cyclic query is handled as an Extend followed by an ID filter.
E.g. MATCH (a)-[e1]->(b)-[e2]->(c), (a)-[e3]->(c) and a plan that closes cycle on c

We first cover e1 and e2 with plan S(a)->E(e1,b)->E(e2,c). Then we try to close the cycle with e3 on c.
We append another extend E(e3,c). Note that the two outValueVector e2,c and e3,c should have different identifier in order to apply an ID filter later. We prefix the second c with its rel name, so its identifier becomes e3_c. After that we do a filter on c.id=e3_c.id.

The final plan is S(a)->E(e1,b)->E(e2,c)->E(e3,e3_c)->Filter(c.id=e3_c.id)

Minor change
- Fix bug in Extend outValueVector common label (used to hard code to 0)

title: removing selected position pointing to nullptr when unfiltered
body:
This PR makes selectedPositions point back to INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS const array. This actually has less benefits than I initially anticipated. Specifically, it doesn't allow simplifying the if(inUnfiltered)/else block in filter.cpp and NodeIDVector::discardNulls because if the selectedPositions will be updated, we need to make sure that it's pointing to unique_ptr<sel_t[]> selectedPositionsBuffer; So we need to first change selectedPositions to point to selectedPositionsBuffer but this means we can no longer read from it because where it's pointing to is now unitialized (which was not the case when we had copied the 1, 2, 3, .... positions from INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS. 

However this allows us always directly read from selectedPositions[i] (instead of calling the inline getSelectedPositionAtIdx(i), which ran a comparison first was `return isUnfiltered() ? i : selectedPositions[i]`. So this could have some minor benefits later on and we can remove the  getSelectedPositionAtIdx function.

Currently, we by default take the first column/property in the csv file as the primary key, and that column/property is only used to construct the node id map, but not kept in the storage.

This PR adds the concept of primary key into loader.
Each node csv file now requires that, in the header, one and only one column/property is specified as a primary key.
The way to specifiy a column as a primary key is to append the keyword `PRIMARY` after the data type.
An example is like this:

Frontier data structure + Frontier Extend operator
body:
This PR add a FrontierBag and FrontierSet data structures used by the FrontierExtend operator:
* FrontierBag: A FrontierBag stores (node_offset, multiplicity) pairs such that any two pairs p1 and p2 can have the same node_offset. FrontierBag provides an append(pair) interface. The frontier is a HashTable made of a single main Block and possibly a set of overflow blocks. All blocks are obtained from the Memory manager. The main block has 32 slots and each slot is a SlotNodeIDs struct value while the overflow blocks make up linked lists to handle collisions through chaining once a slot is full. Each (node_offset, multiplicity) pair in the chained linked list is a NodeIDOverflow struct value. A FrontierBag is the data structure used to create frontier local to the thread in the ExtendFrontier operator. The hash function used in append(pair) is % 32 leading the pair to be appended to one of the slot if the slot is not full otherwise follows an overflow pointer. Since the data structure expects a single writer, no coordination is required.
* FrontierSet: A FrontierSet stores (node_offset, multiplicity) pairs such that each pair has a unique node_offset value. The FrontierSet is made by a number of main blocks (each block has 8096 slots and each slot is a SlotNodeIDAndMultiplicity struct value). The number of slots chosen is provided at initialization. The FrontierSet contains further overflow blocks which are used to handle collisions through chaining. The hash function is modulo % numSlots where numSlots is bigger than that from the frontierBag the input pairs are obtained from to ensure that pairs in a slot in a FrontierBag map to unique slots in a global FrontierSet. Since the data structure expects multiple writers, coordination is required when requiring overflow space.
* FrontierExtend Operator: uses openmp as a temporary solution for multithreading. The operator uses a layered approach to create all of the frontiers up to the given upperBound and then outputs node_offsets from lower up to upper layer without merging said layers.

body:
This PR rewrites the projection operator and its mapping in PlanMapper.

A LogicalProjection contains m LogicalExpressions applied to the existing ValueVector(s) up to before the projection in the pipeline.
The projection operator creates a new DataChunks object and new DataChunks to hold the result(s) of the expression. We group the unflat vectors projected as done in prevDataChunks and we create a new DataChunk for flat vectors projected.

When mapping projection from a logical to physical operation. For each expression, we call `appendFlattenOperatorsIfNecessary` and collect a vector representing in its index the expressionPos and its value the dataChunkPos as before the projection. Finally, we clear the physicalOperatorInfo object and refill it with the new DataChunks with the positions normalized from 0 to m'.

**BoundReturnStatement**

- First rewrite * as all variables in scope

body:
This PR makes the following changes:
1. Change some detailed log output from `info` to `debug`, so it hides detailed information from users.
2. Add a testing framework. **NOTICE**: currently, the parsing of test files is not robust enough, so the writing of test files better strictly stick to example files.

The usage of the testing framework requires a user to:
a) write a test file, an example can be found in `test/runner/basic_scan.test`.
```
# description: Basic scan test

-INPUT dataset/tinysnb/
-PARALLELISM 1

-NAME SimpleMatchTest
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)
---- 7

```
One test file is expected to hold a test suite, including a configuration of graph (csv files) input dir (`-INPUT`), parallelism of the processor (`-PARALLELISM`), and also one or multiple queries.
Each query consists of a name, `-NAME`, and the cypher `-QUERY`, followed by the number of tuples, e.g., `---- 1`.
Comparison on the query result is not supported for now (will be added in a later version).

b) add test file into the unittest's data dependency
```
filegroup(
    name = "testfiles",
    srcs = [
        "basic_extend.test",
        "basic_hash_join.test",
        "basic_scan.test",
    ],
    visibility = ["//visibility:public"],
)
```
To read these files in bazel test system, we need add them as data dependency, so they can be exposed and read in the bazel sandbox.

c) create a unittest
```
TEST(BasicTest, BasicScan) {
    TestHelper testHelper;
    ASSERT_TRUE(testHelper.runTest("test/runner/basic_scan.test"));
}
```
To use the test in unittest, we need add a unittest function to specify the path of the test file.

title: Move building hash table to hash join build

This PR optimizes the current parallel hash join implementation:
Instead of updating a globally shared hash table each time we add a dataChunks (in this way, we need to acquire a global hash table lock each time to access the global `htBlocks` and `overflowBlocks`), every hash join build thread keeps a local `htBlocks` and `overflowBlocks` first, then merge into the global one after all local tuples have been materialized.

Each property is assumed to be either nullable (can have null values) or not. We store the billable information in the catalog and pass it to the property readers. If a property can be null the reader updates the output ValueVector's nullMask by comparing each property value to NULL. If the value is NULL, we write TRUE to the null mask.

The PR updates both binary and unary operations by separating the execution of boolean connection operations from the rest and adds IsNull and IsNotNull support.

title: Add PropertyReader and Filter to enumerator

This PR adds propertyReader and filter into enumerator.

**BoundSingleQuery**
This class represents the output of binder and input of enumerator. It contains
- Single QueryGraph that is created by merging multiple input QueryGraphs
- Vector of expressions represents multiple where clause

**Predicate Enumeration**
- Split input WHERE clause by AND
- Apply predicate once a subplan (subgraph) contains all its dependent nodes and rels
  - append missing property readers
  - append filter

**Example**
`MATCH (a)->(b) WHERE a.age > 1 AND b.age > 3 AND a.age < b.age`
Plan1: `S(a) -> PR(a.age) -> Filter(a.age > 1) -> E(b) -> PR(b.age) -> Filter(b.age > 3) -> Filter(a.age < b.age)`
Plan2: `S(b) -> PR(b.age) -> Filter(b.age > 3) -> E(a) -> PR(a.age) -> Filter(a.age > 1) -> Filter(a.age < b.age)`

This PR add LogicalScan And LogicalExtend Enumerator for acyclic queries

**SubgraphPlanTable**
SubgraphPlanTable is a nested map structure to cache enumerated subplans

title: Add simple hash join operator for INNER join type
body:
The hash join is based on the previously implemented #51 .

First, add all data chunks from the build side into the hash table.
Then, probe the hash table to find matched tuples.
Matched tuples are divided into several parts to be reconstructed as the final result dataChunks.

In the final result dataChunks, we keep data chunks from the probe side remain as they are except for the key data chunk.  
The probe side key data chunk will be replaced by (extended to) the `intermediateUnOverflowDataChunk`, which keeps all vectors in the probe side key data chunk, and also vectors from the build side that are not stored as overflow lists in the hash table.
Other overflow payloads in the hash table are read into the` intermediateOverflowDataChunk` as overflow struct values.

The two intermediate data chunks store at most 1024 tuples at a time, which will be flat in the final result dataChunks, and the overflow lists are copied into the result dataChunks as separate unflat data chunks.

title: Add parser for MatchClause
body:
This PR adds open cypher grammar and parser for MATCH clause.
### Grammar
We use the same grammar as [open cypher](https://s3.amazonaws.com/artifacts.opencypher.org/Cypher.g4) but remove features that are not yet supported. Eventually we should add these features back.
**Grammar Removed**
- Un-directed and bi-directed edge. E.g. `(a)-[e1]-(b),  (a)<-[e1]->(b)`
- Multi node labels. E.g. `(a:Person:Student)`
- Multi edge types. E.g. `[e1:knows|:likes]`

### Parser
Parser class structure closely follows open cypher grammar.
- NodePattern: `(a:Person)`
  - name, type 
- RelPattern: `-[e1:knows]->`
  - name, label, direction
- PatternElementChain: `-[e1:knows]->(b:Student)`
  - relPattern, nodePattern 
- PatternElement: `(a:Person) -[e1:knows]->(b:Student)  -[e2]->(c) `
  -  nodePattern, vector\<PatternElementChain\>
- MatchStatement: `MATCH ..., ...`
  - vector\<PatternElement\> 
- SingleQuery `MATCH ... MATCH ...`
  - vector\<MatchStatement\>

title: Add QueryProcessor with Sync Task System
body:
The PR adds a QueryProcessor acting as a Task system. The processor given a plan and a number of threads creates Task(s) which are pushed to a queue. Each thread is stealing from the Queue and once all threads executed and are done, a notifyAll done is called.

Currently this implementation is synchronous i.e., makes the main thread block using wait() till the queue is empty and all threads executed which would work fine for a CLI. I spent time exploring futures and async execution and made some plans to incorporate it in the future.
